9/7/25 - **_Heritage_** - The expertise of the Fondation de la Sauvegarde de l’Art français (French Heritage Preservation Foundation) and the essential role it plays in preserving the thousands of endangered churches throughout France have been officially recognized by the Ministry of Culture, which signed a three-year framework agreement with the foundation on 4 July.
Chaired by Olivier de Rohan-Chabot, the foundation may now take part in the national fundraising campaign launched in 2023 in support of rural religious heritage.
This campaign was initially entrusted exclusively to the Fondation du patrimoine (Heritage Foundation).
It has now been extended, through the enactment of the 2025 Finance Act, to all foundations recognized as being of public utility – and in particular to the Sauvegarde de l’Art français.
The funds raised are intended to finance restoration, maintenance, and conservation work on religious buildings – of all faiths – in municipalities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants.

An exceptional measure allows each donor to benefit from a 75% tax deduction, up to a maximum of 1,000 euros per year, which fortunately runs counter to the report by the Inspection générale des finances (General Inspectorate of Finance), which proposed reducing – or even eliminating – tax incentives for sponsorship (see the article).
For decades, the Fondation pour la Sauvegarde de l’Art français has been working to safeguard religious heritage.
Whether a simple chapel or a building classified as a Historic Monument, each case is examined by volunteer professionals – monuments historiques chief architects and art historians.
This preservation naturally involves the restoration of the buildings, but also includes educating the public.
The foundation is also concerned with the artworks housed in these buildings, thanks to the campaign Le Plus Grand Musée de France (The Largest Museum in France), launched in 2013 (see the article).

Olivier de Rohan-Chabot points out that religious heritage alone accounts for half of all French heritage, and that the threat it faces stems not only from a lack of maintenance – and therefore the structural deterioration of buildings – but also from the declining number of worshippers and inhabitants.

Indeed, despite support from the State and local authorities in financing restoration work, the remaining costs are often too high for the municipalities, which highlights the importance of public sponsorship.
To encourage broader participation in this campaign, this heritage – so often forgotten – must be made better known.
On the occasion of the upcoming European Heritage Days, a nationwide popular vote will be launched.

Giving the public a choice means involving them in the campaign and encouraging them to donate: French citizens will thus be able to select one endangered religious building, from a shortlist of three in each region chosen with the help of the DRAC (Direction régionale des affaires culturelles, or Regional Directorate of Cultural Affairs).
Donations can then be made either for the selected building or more generally for rural heritage.
And since choosing means leaving others behind, let us hope that the churches not selected this time will still be standing when the next fundraising campaign comes around...
